    #89927. Tech Report: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2338 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Criminal law is constitutional law

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite.
    • Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.
    • It has been revealed that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

    Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law.

    It has been revealed that every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

    It has been revealed that “[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

    In a recent development, but why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”.

    Thus, a fundamental premise of criminal law, Winship, is constitutional law too. Moreover, and just by the way, Winship demonstrates that the “incorporation” theory of the 14th Amendment’s Due Process Clause (that is, applying the Bill of Rights to the states) is not limited to concepts stated expressly in the Bill of Rights itself – as “proof beyond a reasonable doubt” is not. Critics of non-textual constitutional rights – like privacy, a right to travel, a right to refuse medical treatment (like mask wearing?), or even a right to terminate a pregnancy – must confront the application of their literalist theory to proof beyond a reasonable doubt, too. For this reason, I also teach Winship in every constitutional law class.

    There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution.

    Industry observers note that this sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

    According to recent reports, so the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.).

    Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure.

    Three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

    One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

    Industry observers note that why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

    (Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.).

    In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

    And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution.

    Industry observers note that in his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then Upcoming York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

    Industry observers note that criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

    According to recent reports, in addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it claims,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

    For example, Griswold v. Connecticut recognized a constitutional right to privacy in the criminal law context, resting in part (and almost entirely for three justices) on the Ninth Amendment. Less controversially, perhaps, Chief Justice Warren Burger later invoked the amendment in the 1980 case of Richmond Newspapers v. Virginia to support an “unarticulated” constitutional right for the public (and the press) to attend criminal trials. And in 2000, even Justice Antonin Scalia agreed (in a solo dissent to Troxel v. Granville, a non-criminal case) that the Ninth Amendment recognizes unenumerated rights. When you tell your Thanksgiving dinner companions that criminal law is constitutional law, don’t forget the Ninth Amendment.

    So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law.

    Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

    Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law.

    By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

    Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

    According to recent reports, immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

    In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

    Sources indicate that last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

    Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

    Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/.

    #89926. 2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1091 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abajournal ↗ Open Full Page

    2 Montgomery County magnet stories raise 1 question about access

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1091 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.
    • Sources indicate that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences.
    • Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an key issue: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    “Minorities in Magnets” was the winner of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition.

    Sources indicate that A high school filmmaker saw a problem in Montgomery County, Maryland’s selective programs: Lack of representation of students of color had an impact on their educational experiences. At nearly the same time, a lawsuit challenging admissions to the county’s middle school magnet programs reached the U.S. Supreme Court.

    Although these stories involve different programs and raise different questions, they share an key issue: How do we determine whether an admissions system provides fair access to educational opportunities, and what evidence should matter?

    The ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice recognized Minorities in Magnets, directed by Toftaa Fedhaa, as the first place winner of the section’s 2026 High School Civil Rights Film Competition. Her film explores the experiences of students of color in the Montgomery County Public Schools’ high school magnet programs and the effects of their underrepresentation.

    Separately, on Oct. 19, the Supreme Court agreed to hear Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education. The case concerns admissions to four selective middle school magnet programs, not the high school programs discussed in the film.

    While the court did not rule on whether the district’s admissions policy is discriminatory, it agreed to consider a narrower legal question about the evidence plaintiffs must present when challenging a facially neutral admissions policy as racially discriminatory.

    Sources indicate that the Association for Education Fairness alleges that Montgomery County’s admissions policies intentionally disadvantaged Asian American students. The school district maintains that its admissions system is designed to provide equitable access to rigorous educational opportunities.

    Industry observers note that after initially challenging a “field test,” the plaintiffs challenged a revised lottery-based system introduced for the 2021-2022 school year. That system screened students for their potential to benefit from enriched instruction and then used a lottery to assign students to magnet programs or enriched instruction at their neighborhood schools.

    The federal district court dismissed the challenge to the revised plan, finding that the plaintiffs had not adequately alleged discriminatory effect or intent. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, affirmed, applying circuit precedent on disparate impact allegations.

    The Supreme Court will now consider whether a plaintiff challenging a facially neutral admissions policy must demonstrate that the affected group experienced an aggregate “disparate impact” compared with its share of the applicant pool.

    Industry observers note that put simply, “disparate impact” refers to a policy that produces unequal outcomes for a particular group, even when the policy does not expressly classify individuals by race. An equal protection challenge also raises the question of discriminatory purpose.

    Recent findings suggest that the court’s decision will address the legal standards governing these types of claims and whether a particular showing of aggregate impact is required before such a claim may proceed, not whether Montgomery County’s policy ultimately violates the Constitution. The court has not yet decided the merits of the case.

    The film underscores why the conversation should not only focus exclusively on admissions policies, statistics and legal standards but should also consider the voices and experiences of students.

    The file and the lawsuit should not be confused or treated as evidence of one another. They involve different grade levels, programs and legal questions. The experiences described in the film do not establish what happened in the middle school admissions process, just as the allegations in the lawsuit do not resolve the concerns raised by high school students.

    Although selective educational programs can open doors to advanced coursework, specialized instruction and opportunities that shape a student’s academic future, simply making a program available to everyone does not necessarily mean everyone has an equal opportunity to participate.

    We must also consider who knows these programs exist, how students are identified and encouraged to apply, what barriers may discourage participation, and whether students feel represented and welcome once they are admitted.

    It has been revealed that these are crucial questions for educators, families, policymakers and communities to consider. They may also inform legal analysis, although the applicable legal standards determine what evidence is relevant to a particular claim.

    For lawyers, the Supreme Court case highlights the importance of understanding how statistical evidence, applicant pools and allegations of discriminatory intent intersect when challenging facially neutral policies. It also reinforces the need to examine the specific admissions process and how that process may have changed over time. The court’s decision may affect how courts evaluate statistical evidence in challenges to facially neutral admissions policies.

    For school officials, families and advocates, the broader questions are equally important:.

    • How are students identified and informed about selective educational opportunities?

    • What criteria determine eligibility and admission?

    • Are admissions outcomes regularly examined across schools and student populations?

    • Are the policies and measures used to assess access transparent and understandable?

    These questions deserve attention regardless of how the Supreme Court ultimately resolves the legal matter before it.

    The case is also a reminder that we must distinguish between allegations in a lawsuit, a school district’s stated reasons for its policies, procedural court decisions, and a final ruling on the merits. Understanding those distinctions is essential to an informed discussion.

    In a recent development, the winning film, Minorities in Magnets, brings student perspectives into a debate that is often reduced to admissions criteria and demographic statistics. The Supreme Court will address a specific legal question about the evidence required in an equal protection challenge.

    In a recent development, neither alone answers the broader question of what meaningful educational opportunity should look like. But they invite a broader conversation about how communities define opportunity, how they measure access, and how they respond when students say the system is not working for them.

    As lawyers and members of our communities, we have an obligation to listen, ask difficult questions, and examine whether the systems we create are providing genuine opportunities for all students.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, educational access is about more than who gets admitted. It is also about who gets the opportunity to succeed, who feels that they belong, and whether every student has a fair chance to reach their full potential.

    Mario A. Sulllivan is the immediate past chair of the ABA Section of Civil Rights and Social Justice and a name partner at Johnson & Sullivan in Chicago.

    This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

    American gun buyers claim top manufacturers run an âunlawful price fixing cartelâ that extracts profits through nationwide enforcement of restrictions on how much retailers can discount firearms.

    (CN) â An Alabama gun buyer brought a class action against six of the nation’s largest gunmakers accusing them of conspiring with major hunting retailers like Bass Pro Shops to fix prices of guns sold to American consumers.

    Filed in Upcoming Hampshire federal court on Monday, the class action is led by William Foster, a Bass Pro Shops customer who says he and other buyers were overcharged on firearms purchases due to a price-fixing conspiracy between the gun makers, wholesalers and retailers.

    âThe increasing pace of firearm sales in the 2010s and 2020s broke previous patterns and indicated that defendants and others in the industry could maintain strong firearm demand, no matter how inflated the prices became as a result of the minimum advertised price conspiracy,â Foster wrote in the complaint.

    The proposed class of American gun buyers notes the minimum advertised price policy that kept the prices of retail guns artificially inflated was enforced against retailers and distributors through warnings, suspension of shipments, loss of authorized-dealer status or termination of the resellerâs access to the manufacturerâs products.

    Foster targets Sig Sauer, Smith & Wesson, Ruger, Glock, FN Firearms and Beretta in his complaint along with Bass Pro Shops and Cabela’s. He points to the competing gunmakersâ exchange of sensitive information and invitations to collude as evidence of their participation in an âunlawful price-fixing cartel.â.

    The formal price-fixing policy was instituted by Sig Sauer in 2015, according to Foster, and memorialized to the industry during a National Association of Sporting Goods Wholesalers webinar titled âListen and Learn: Obtaining Customer Feedback and Input to Grow Sales and Profits.â.

    âThe fact that Sig Sauer was voluntarily speaking to an audience of its direct competitors, revealing proprietary internal data and pricing strategies, and emphasizing that the companyâs decision on pricing was based on collective input, sent one unmistakable message: We have instituted minimum advertised price and it is now safe for others to do the same,â the buyers wrote in the complaint.

    The class action was filed in New Hampshire federal district court because Sig Sauer, originally a Swiss tech giant, is headquartered in Newington, New Hampshire.

    The three-count complaint is comprised of violations of federal antitrust, state antitrust and consumer protection laws, and one count of unjust enrichment.

    Representatives for the gun companies and retailers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday morning.

    The gun safety advocacy group Guns Down America released a report in July similarly finding evidence of decadeslong vertical coordination between retailers and gun manufacturers to artificially fix prices above what the market might otherwise support.

    In a recent development, âThe gun industry in the United States has been remarkably successful at resisting policy changes and business reforms that would save lives,â wrote Hudson Munoz, executive director of Guns Down America, in a statement announcing the report. âFor decades, a major driver of that success has been overlooked: the gun industryâs cartel-like approach to pricing firearms. Enforcement that eliminates vertical agreements would improve public policy and, through competition, deliver safer products from better companies.â.

    The report, titled âThe Price is Wrong,â found firearms manufacturers, distributors, retailers and trade associations share information and resources to enforce mandatory price floors.

    Costa Rica has been celebrated for reversing decades of deforestation.

    PUERTO VIEJO DE TALAMANCA, Costa Rica (AP) â Behind a beachfront hotel on Costa Ricaâs Caribbean coast, conservationists are installing rope bridges between trees, creating pathways for sloths in a landscape increasingly shared with tourists, hotels and other development.

    It has been revealed that for sloths, even a small gap in the forest canopy can be dangerous. Unable to jump between trees like monkeys, the slow-moving mammals are often forced to descend to the ground, where they risk being attacked by dogs, struck by vehicles or electrocuted on power lines.

    To help them move safely through the treetops, the Sloth Conservation Foundation has installed approximately 410 rope bridges often across areas divided by roads and buildings.

    âThe wildlife bridges that we install are just made from single ropes, which donât look very elaborate, but for arboreal species, they work,â noted Rebecca Cliffe, a British zoologist who founded the organization and has spent nearly two decades studying sloths.

    âIt is a lifeline to cross a gap that they otherwise couldnât cross.â.

    In a recent development, costa Rica has been celebrated for reversing decades of deforestation, with forest cover increasing from an estimated 21% of its territory in 1987 to 59%, according to a 2023 report by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. But the recovery has not eliminated habitat fragmentation, as development and tourism infrastructure continue to put pressure on coastal ecosystems.

    Sloths spend much of their lives suspended from branches, relying on familiar routes between trees to find food and shelter.

    Even a gap of 2 or 3 meters (about 7 to 10 feet) between neighboring tree canopies can force a sloth to find another way across, a phenomenon Cliffe calls âmicrofragmentation.â.

    âTheyâre creatures of habit,â she said, explaining that sloths tend to follow routes learned early in life, even as their surroundings change.

    Cliffe began experimenting with wildlife bridges after working at the Sloth Sanctuary nearly two decades ago, where she repeatedly saw animals arriving with injuries from dog attacks, vehicles and electrical cables.

    âI thought, well, the sloths just need a safer way to get somewhere,â she noted.

    With little funding, she began installing single ropes between trees. Cameras monitoring some of the bridges have since recorded more than 22,000 wildlife crossings, including animals other than sloths, Cliffe mentioned.

    Today, her team travels to sites where sloths have been spotted, including hotels and other properties along the Caribbean coast. At one beachfront hotel in Puerto Viejo, workers installed bridges among trees near an area frequented by tourists.

    The project also involves planting trees and working with property owners to restore natural connections between neighboring plots. But the bridges are not permanent. Cliffe said ropes deteriorate after about four or five years in tropical conditions, requiring replacement.

    Although Costa Rica has regained substantial forest cover, much of that growth has occurred on former pastureland within landscapes fragmented by decades of agricultural expansion, said Carlos Morera Beita, a geographer at the National University of Costa Rica.

    Morera stated sloths have demonstrated greater adaptability than previously believed, using tree-lined pastures, living fences and riverside vegetation to move between forest patches.

    Recent findings suggest that but these connections remain essential. Without them, even recovering forests can leave sloth populations isolated, limiting their access to food, mates and shelter.

    Rope bridges can help animals cross specific obstacles, Morera stated, but long-term conservation requires protecting existing forests, restoring biological corridors and ensuring fresh development does not further fragment habitats.

    At the Sloth Sanctuary of Costa Rica on the outskirts of the small town of Penshurst, tourists observe sloths that cannot return to the wild because of severe injuries, disabilities or the loss of their mothers before they learned the skills needed to survive independently.

    Inside, founder Judy Avey-Arroyoâs bedroom is filled with sloth memorabilia, from stuffed animals and paintings to lamps and ornaments. She and her daughter even have sloth tattoos.

    The youngest are kept in incubators and fed milk, while older babies are given leaves, outdoor exercise and opportunities to learn to climb.

    Sources indicate that but Avey-Arroyo noted replacing a mother is nearly impossible. Young sloths spend about a year learning which leaves are safe to eat, which plants to avoid and how to navigate the forest along familiar routes. Mothers also teach them which leaves to seek out when suffering from parasites, she said.

    Without that knowledge, even apparently healthy orphaned sloths can struggle to survive in the wild.

    For Avey-Arroyo, whose work began after she and her husband rescued an orphaned sloth named Buttercup, knowing that some animals will never return to the forest is the hardest part of running the sanctuary.

    Climate change could worsen the effects of fragmentation, as rising temperatures and prolonged droughts alter the conditions sloths depend on.

    Small forest patches are more exposed to heat, wind and lower humidity than continuous forests, Morera remarked, reducing habitat quality even where trees remain standing.

    It has been revealed that sloths rely on their surroundings to regulate body temperature and metabolism, moving between shaded and sunlit areas of the forest. Cliffe mentioned prolonged periods of extreme heat can deplete their limited energy reserves, while cold conditions can disrupt digestion.

    The concern has prompted conservationists to look beyond rope bridges toward broader habitat restoration, including planting trees that provide shade.

    It has been revealed that âItâs not just bridges that are going to save sloths,â Cliffe noted. âYouâve got to provide the connectivity, you also have to provide the thermal refuges.â.

    Despite their popularity as symbols of Costa Ricaâs wildlife, scientists lack reliable estimates of how many sloths live in the countryâs forests or how their populations are changing.

    Industry observers note that cliffeâs organization is experimenting with thermal imaging drones, trained detection dogs and field surveys to improve estimates. She said two rescue centers in the region receive approximately three sloths a day, although historical data is needed to determine whether rescues are increasing.

    In coastal communities like Puerto Viejo de Talamanca, conservationists hope the bridges will eventually be replaced by trees growing close enough together for sloths to move freely through the canopy.

    For Cliffe, protecting sloths ultimately comes down to the collective impact of small actions, whether planting a tree, preserving a branch or installing a simple rope bridge.

    Sources indicate that âItâs the cumulative power of many individual actions,â she remarked. âThatâs what really gives me hope.â.

    Supreme Court considers whether bans on semiautomatic rifles violate Second Amendment

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Abajournal

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in June 2025, the U.S.
    • “Given that millions of Americans own AR–15s and that a significant majority of the states allow possession of those rifles, [the challengers] have a strong argument that AR–15s are in ‘common use’ by law-abiding citizens and therefore are protected by the Second Amendment under [District of Columbia v.] Heller,” Kavanaugh wrote in a statement respecting the denial.
    • Heller is the court’s landmark 2008 decision that upheld the right of individuals to keep a firearm in the home for self-defense and established that the Second Amendment must be interpreted in light of constitutional text, history and tradition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 24, 2026, 11:12 am CST.

    Sources indicate that in June 2025, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take up a case challenging Maryland’s prohibition on AR-15 semiautomatic rifles, with three justices dissenting from the denial of review and a fourth, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, stopping just short of that.

    “Given that millions of Americans own AR–15s and that a significant majority of the states allow possession of those rifles, [the challengers] have a strong argument that AR–15s are in ‘common use’ by law-abiding citizens and therefore are protected by the Second Amendment under [District of Columbia v.] Heller,” Kavanaugh wrote in a statement respecting the denial.

    Heller is the court’s landmark 2008 decision that upheld the right of individuals to keep a firearm in the home for self-defense and established that the Second Amendment must be interpreted in light of constitutional text, history and tradition.

    Kavanaugh suggested the court might be assisted in addressing such bans in the future by rulings in pending challenges to similar state laws in several federal appeals courts.

    “Additional petitions for certiorari will likely be before this court shortly, and, in my view, this court should and presumably will address the AR–15 problem soon, in the next term or two,” he wrote.

    It has been revealed that kavanaugh was right on both counts. Next week, the justices will hear arguments in two cases raising the constitutionality of AR-15s “and similar semiautomatic rifles.”.

    “This case has massive stakes, symbolically,” says Adam Winkler, a professor at the University of California at Los Angeles School of Law and the author of the 2011 book Gunfight: The Battle Over the Right to Bear Arms in America.

    “The assault weapons bans have been at the very center of the gun debate ever since the Newtown shooting in 2012,” he indicates, referring to the mass shooting at the Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, in which a perpetrator using an AR-15-style rifle killed 20 first graders and six school staff members.

    “This is the first time the Supreme Court is ruling on the availability of such a high-profile firearm,” Winkler notes.

    On Dec. 2, the Supreme Court will take up a challenge to Connecticut’s move, soon after the Sandy Hook mass shooting, to outlaw AR-15 and similar platform semiautomatic rifles. That case, Grant v. Higgins, is consolidated with the lead case, Khaya v. Cook County, in which the justices will consider a 1993 ordinance in prohibiting AR-15-style rifles in Cook County, Illinois, which includes Chicago.

    In practical terms, the Cook County ordinance has been superseded by an Illinois statute enacted after a mass shooting at the 2022 Fourth of July parade in the Chicago suburb of Highland Park, in which seven people were killed and 50 wounded.

    Besides Connecticut and Illinois, 11 other states prohibit AR-15-style weapons, and the fate of those laws are on the table in the consolidated cases before the justices.

    The Connecticut law was challenged by two gun rights groups and several individuals, who argue that both Heller and the high court’s 2022 decision in Newly introduced York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen necessitated a finding that AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles are protected arms that cannot be banned consistent with the Second Amendment.

    (Bruen held that the states could not prevent law-abiding citizens with self-defense needs from carrying firearms in public, and it reiterated Heller’s history and tradition test.).

    The 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at New York upheld Connecticut’s law in 2025, saying governments may restrict weapons that were “unusually dangerous.”.

    The decades-old Cook County ordinance was challenged in 2021. The 7th Circuit at Chicago in 2025 applied its own 2023 decision that preliminarily upheld the Illinois statute.

    The Trump administration, which is supporting the challenges in the Supreme Court, cites statistics that at least 16 million Americans own AR-15s, and that some 28 million such rifles are in circulation in the country.

    The challengers cite the 16 million figure but also other statistics suggesting that as many as 26 million Americans own AR-15s or similar weapons.

    “If the Second Amendment is to have any teeth at all, at bare minimum, it must include protecting the most common arms in the country,” notes Bill Sack, the senior director of legal operations for the Second Amendment Foundation, a Bellevue, Washington-based group that is a plaintiff in and the chief organizer of the Connecticut and Cook County cases.

    The challengers argue that no valid historical principle under the analytical test unveiled in Heller and refined in Bruen justifies the bans on AR-15-style rifles.

    Industry observers note that “Our litigation strategy … is making sure that the types of arms that Americans choose to use for all lawful purposes are available to them,” Sack indicates. “Long guns … are just as notable to the exercise of the Second Amendment as handguns are.”.

    In a recent development, erin E. Murphy, a partner with Clement & Murphy who helped win the Bruen case, notes there is another key way for the court to look at history in the case.

    Recent findings suggest that “Semiautomatic rifles and semiautomatic handguns have been around for well over a century,” notes Murphy, who wrote an amicus brief for the National Shooting Sports Foundation in support of the challengers. “I think that history is going to matter to the court.”.

    Connecticut cites the string of deadly mass shootings at schools and other places involving AR-15-style weapons.

    In a recent development, “Tragically, real-world experience confirms the AR-15’s singular dangerousness: From Sandy Hook to Las Vegas to Parkland to Uvalde, shooters have used the AR-15 or similar weapons in the vast majority of mass-casualty shootings this century,” notes the merits brief filed by William Tong, the Connecticut attorney general, and Elizabeth B. Prelogar, a former U.S. solicitor general.

    While serving under then-President Joe Biden, Prelogar argued United States v. Rahimi, in which the court in 2024 upheld a federal ban on firearm possession by individuals subject to domestic violence restraining orders. Though hired by Connecticut, Prelogar will represent both that state and Cook County in oral arguments before the court.

    Connecticut argues that legislatures going back to medieval England have chosen to ban unusually dangerous weapons, such as English crossbows, colonial trap guns and 19th century Bowie knives.

    “Over the centuries, the march of technological advancement has increased the lethality of weapons, and governments have consistently responded by outlawing weapons with characteristics that make them more lethal than their contemporary peers,” Tong and Prelogar argue.

    Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, a Democrat, emphasizes the importance of prohibiting assault weapons in her jurisdiction of 5 million people.

    “It’s not a coincidence that 11 of the most populous states in the country have a ban on assault weapons,” Burke indicates in an interview. “And the reason for that is because the capabilities of these weapons are not appropriate for densely populated urban areas.”.

    Sources indicate that bullets fired from an AR-15 “have a significantly greater lethal capability,” she adds. “When someone is shot with an AR-15, the damage to the human body is so significant that it’s much more likely to be lethal.”.

    It has been revealed that there was some eleventh-hour drama in the Cook County case, with the lead plaintiff, Cutberto Viramontes, asking to be dismissed from the case. His motion did not explain why.

    In response, Cook County argued that the only other individual challenger in the case, Christopher Khaya, lacks standing because he does not seek to own an AR-15 but instead an IMI Galil-Israeli rifle that is modeled on the AK-47. Because of that, Burke claims she was obligated to file a suggestion of mootness for the case, which would leave only the Connecticut law at issue.

    Sack of the Second Amendment Foundation declined to say why Viramontes was seeking out of the case, but his group filed a response arguing that the IMI Galil-Israeli rifle is covered by the question presented in the case, and that the second challenger now also seeks to own an AR-15.

    Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 23, the Supreme Court agreed to dismiss Viramontes from the Cook County case, and designated Khaya as the lead petitioner. A day later, the court mentioned it would consider the mootness question at oral argument.

    In a recent development, winkler of the UCLA School of Law says the central matter in the case, while generating a lot of heat, may be of more importance symbolically than in reality. Despite their use in several high-profile mass shootings, AR-15s are relatively rarely used in criminal activity, he says. And with only 11 states prohibiting them, they remain legal in most of the country.

    But if the court upholds these bans, that will energize gun rights activists, he says.

    But “if it strikes them down, it will motivate gun rights activists to become even more mobilized politically,” possibly prodding them to refocus on other ideas for reducing gun violence more broadly, Winkler indicates.

    In either event, Winkler claims, “whatever the Supreme Court does here will necessarily get far more public attention than other recent decisions by the court on the Second Amendment.”.

    #89910. The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2208 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    The Supreme Court and profanity

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2208 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, around 2 p.m.
    • The station later stated it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl.
    • Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, around 2 p.m. on October 30, 1973, John Douglas was driving with his 15-year-old son when he heard a litany of profanity come over the radio. Upcoming York’s WBAI, a nonprofit radio station, was airing a program on modern attitudes toward language. Near the end, the station played George Carlin’s “Filthy Words” routine, which begins with the comedian saying he’d been thinking about “the words you couldn’t say on the public airwaves; the ones you definitely wouldn’t say, ever.” He went on to repeat those words several times, contrasting them with words like “bastards,” “hell,” and “damn,” which were mostly acceptable, and showing how even some of his list of seven were perfectly fine in other contexts. His point was to show the absurdity of profanity.

    The station later stated it had chosen Carlin’s routine because it was an “incisive satirical view of the subject under discussion,” in the style of other great satirists like Mark Twain or Mort Sahl. Carlin, the station explained, was doing more than “mouthing obscenities.” He was “using words to satirize as harmless and essentially silly our attitudes towards those words.”.

    Before playing the routine, the host had warned that it included language some listeners might find offensive and suggested they return in 15 minutes if they were inclined toward offense. But about a month later, John Douglas complained to the Federal Communications Commission about the transmission which he noted was “garbage” and had been broadcast in the presence of his “young son.” He was the only listener to do so. A member of Morality in Media who frequently listened to the station to “see how far” they’d go, Douglas later acknowledged that he had laughed out loud at the bit but “did not appreciate WBIA’s ‘smart-alecky’ on-air provocations.”.

    The previous year, Carlin had been arrested after performing an earlier version of the same routine, but a judge threw out the charge. This time, the FCC found the broadcast “indecent,” and put its order in the station’s license file.

    That order ended up before the Supreme Court.

    It has been revealed that early in its order, the FCC acknowledged that Congress had forbade it from censoring broadcasts. But Congress had also prohibited the broadcast of “obscene, indecent, or profane” language, and the Commission thought Carlin’s broadcast fit the bill. In the FCC’s view, the ban on “indecent” language covered not just obscenity, but also patently offensive language when there was a reasonable risk of children listening. Late at night, when children were unlikely to be listening, the same material might be okay if it appeared in a work of serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

    Two commissioners thought even that was too permissive. Charlotte Reid believed “this language to be totally inappropriate for broadcast at anytime” and thought the commission’s standard did “not go far enough.” Commissioner James Quello took much the same view. “Garbage is garbage,” he wrote, whether children were listening or not.

    It has been revealed that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, however, set aside the order in a 2-1 vote, with one judge believing it violated the statutory ban on censorship and the other saying it violated the First Amendment. The FCC appealed to the Supreme Court.

    It has been revealed that at oral argument, which was held in April of 1978, several justices made their distaste for Carlin’s bit plain. When Pacifica’s lawyer stressed that the station had warned listeners beforehand and aired the monologue as part of an educational program about language, Chief Justice Warren Burger incredulously asked, “This is educational in your view?” And when counsel defended the material’s artistic value, Justice Thurgood Marshall responded, “Well, I’m not an expert, but if that’s artistic, deliver me.” Justice William Rehnquist, for his part, tested the limits of Pacifica’s position with a hypothetical involving a single four-letter word repeated for an hour. Would the FCC be powerless to prohibit that? Justice John Paul Stevens, however, seemed troubled by the potential reach of the FCC’s position, given that the prohibition on indecency could be enforced through criminal law.

    One striking exchange concerned the Justice Department’s position to argue separately, and more narrowly, than the FCC. The solicitor general’s office urged that the First Amendment prevented the government from barring particular words outright for a substantial part of the day without regard to context, even if the FCC could constitutionally regulate “indecency” to some extent. Rehnquist sharply asked why the Justice Department was arguing against the FCC, what interest it had in seeking a narrow construction of an act of Congress, and whether the solicitor general, as the government’s lawyer, could ever argue that an act of Congress was unconstitutional.

    Industry observers note that justice Lewis Powell also pressed the DOJ on the reasons behind its departure from the FCC, noting that the DOJ had supported the FCC in the court below. “That is true, and that is an embarrassment to us,” Deputy Solicitor General Louis Claiborne acknowledged, suggesting it was because the matter had been handled there by the Antitrust Division rather than the Criminal Division. Another explanation, which he did not mention, was that the administration had changed.

    The court ultimately ruled 5-4 that the FCC could constitutionally treat this broadcast as “indecent” under the governing statute, and that the government could constitutionally prohibit indecency even though it fell short of legal obscenity. Stevens wrote for Burger, Justice Harry Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist, having apparently struggled with the case and flip-flopped before settling against Pacifica. The Commission had treated the piece as a nuisance, and, as the court had observed in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co., a nuisance could be as simple as “a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” He concluded that “when the Commission finds that a pig has entered the parlor, the exercise of its regulatory power does not depend on proof that the pig is obscene.” Though the holding expanded the government’s power to regulate speech, Stevens emphasized broadcasting’s pervasive presence in the home and its accessibility to children, the fact the piece was broadcast during the daytime, and the narrowness of the holding. He did not address late night broadcasts or the “occasional expletive.”.

    Stevens had only three votes for some parts of his opinion. Powell, joined by Blackmun, wrote separately to object to Stevens’ suggestion that the level of protection that speech receives should depend on a judge’s perception of that speech’s value. For them, the combination of repeated, patently offensive language, an afternoon broadcast, and children’s ready access was enough to resolve the case. Powell also addressed the concern that the decision could end up “reduc[ing] the adult population . . . to [hearing] only what is fit for children”: adults could buy tapes or hear the same words at theaters.

    Justice Potter Stewart dissented, joined by Justices William Brennan, Byron White, and Marshall. Stewart would have resolved the case on statutory grounds. He read “indecent” to reach only obscene material, and everyone agreed that Carlin’s monologue fell outside that category. His opinion recalled his concurrence in Jacobellis v. Ohio, where he voted to overturn an obscenity conviction for showing a French film with an explicit love scene. Stewart understood obscenity narrowly, but declined to define it, famously observing in that case, “I know it when I see it, and the motion picture involved in this case is not that.”.

    It has been revealed that brennan wrote a separate dissent, joined by Marshall, that went further. He agreed with Stewart on the statute and said he would ordinarily refrain from addressing the constitutional question, but he found “the Court’s misapplication of fundamental First Amendment principles so patent, and its attempt to impose its notions of propriety on the whole of the American people so misguided,” that he was “unable to remain silent.”.

    It has been revealed that brennan disputed the analogy between a radio broadcast and an intrusion into the home. Listeners voluntarily turn on the radio, and they can voluntarily turn it off. In perhaps his sharpest passage, he wrote:.

    Brennan also questioned the majority’s reliance on protecting children. He read the court’s precedents as allowing the government to shield children from material that was obscene as to them. In his view, Carlin’s routine fell outside that category. Keeping it off the radio during the afternoon cut off access for adults as well as children. And while the majority had invoked parents’ right to raise their children as they saw fit, Brennan thought the FCC had somewhat ironically made the choice for them.

    Finally, he remained unconvinced that the court’s reasoning would reach only cases like Carlin’s. Among the things it could sweep in were “literary works, novels, poems, and plays by the likes of Shakespeare, Joyce, Hemingway, Ben Jonson, Henry Fielding, Robert Burns, and Chaucer,” “a good deal of political speech, such as the Nixon tapes,” and even portions of the Bible. In his view, the public, and not the court, should have the power to weed out “worthless and offensive” speech in a marketplace “unsullied by the censor’s hand.”.

    Brennan and Marshall had joined together in another Supreme Court opinion involving the F-word. In Cohen v. California, they joined Justice John Harlan II’s opinion protecting the right to wear a jacket emblazoned with “Fuck the Draft.” Stewart joined it too (not surprisingly, Burger and Blackmun dissented). Brennan brought Cohen straight into his Pacifica dissent; as he made clear, changing the words can change what the speaker communicates, something that applies especially well to Carlin because the taboo words were themselves the subject of the routine. And Brennan thought telling listeners to buy a record or pay to see Carlin live missed what it meant to hear the routine on the radio.

    Recent findings suggest that in closing, Brennan wrote that the majority had only “confirm[ed] Carlin’s prescience as a social commentator.” (It was interesting that Marshall, who sounded distinctly unimpressed by the claim of artistic merit at oral argument, joined him, perhaps especially here.) As Brennan pointed out, Carlin had made fun of the rules about which words you could say on the air, and the court had exemplified the very attitude he was satirizing. To top it all off: Appended to the opinion is the transcript of Carlin’s routine, giving his “indecent” words a permanent home in the U.S. Reports.

    Recent findings suggest that at the 2002 Billboard Music Awards on Fox, Cher dispatched the critics who’d spent decades predicting her downfall with “So f*** ’em.” At the 2003 awards, Nicole Richie asked whether anyone had tried getting cow manure out of a Prada purse, then used the F-word to describe how hard it was. The next year, after Bono called U2’s Golden Globe win “really, really f***ing brilliant,” the FCC declared that even a single expletive could be indecent, and it later applied that approach to the two earlier Fox broadcasts.

    Recent findings suggest that in 2009, the Supreme Court took up the dispute in FCC v. Fox Television Stations. Writing for a 5-4 majority, Justice Antonin Scalia held that the FCC had adequately explained its change in policy under the Administrative Procedure Act, leaving the First Amendment question open. Justice Clarence Thomas joined the majority but wrote separately to question Pacifica’s holding. On remand, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit struck down the policy as unconstitutionally vague.

    The case returned to the Supreme Court in 2012 and all eight participating justices agreed on the result (Justice Sonia Sotomayor recused herself). Justice Anthony Kennedy’s opinion held that the FCC had failed to give Fox fair notice that fleeting expletives could trigger an indecency finding, but once again left both Pacifica and the First Amendment question open. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote separately to say that Pacifica was wrong from the start and deserved reconsideration. But while the court has had several cases involving curse words since, it has yet to take up the question directly.

    In 2004, the FCC dismissed complaints related to the airing of Saving Private Ryan on the basis that the film’s curse words helped convey the soldiers’ experience. But just two years later, it slapped a station with $15,000 in fines for airing a Martin Scorsese documentary about Blues music that contained profanity. In 2020, the FCC received over 1,300 complaints about Jennifer Lopez and Shakira’s halftime show, though it never took any action against the network. And in February 2026, FCC requested transcripts of Bad Bunny’s Superbowl halftime performance before ultimately finding no violation.

    Half a century after Carlin’s seven dirty words, the FCC’s continued and seemingly arbitrary application of its indecency laws reveals the prescience of Brennan’s dissent and the need to finally answer the question of whether the Constitution prohibits the “dominant culture” from trying to force “groups who do not share its mores to conform to its way of acting, thinking, and speaking.”.

    Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

    California owed water consumers hearings before 2021 drought cutbacks

    • (CN) â The Ninth Circuit on Tuesday reinstated due process claims from a group of Northern California water rights holders who were ordered to curtail their river water diversions in 2021 during a drought emergency.
    • In a unanimous opinion, the three-judge panel reversed a trial judge’s dismissal of the due process claims by Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation, Los Molinos Mutual Water and Peyton Pacific, which between them hold the bulk of the water rights along Deer Creek and Mill Creek, two tributaries of the Sacramento River.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An appellate panel remarked the water companies weren't given a meaningful hearing before the state ordered them to cut back on diversions in 2021.

    (CN) â The Ninth Circuit on Tuesday reinstated due process claims from a group of Northern California water rights holders who were ordered to curtail their river water diversions in 2021 during a drought emergency.

    In a unanimous opinion, the three-judge panel reversed a trial judge’s dismissal of the due process claims by Stanford Vina Ranch Irrigation, Los Molinos Mutual Water and Peyton Pacific, which between them hold the bulk of the water rights along Deer Creek and Mill Creek, two tributaries of the Sacramento River.

    Whereas the trial judge in Sacramento had agreed with the State Water Resources Control Board that its emergency regulations and curtailment orders were “legislative,” the appellate panel concluded they were “adjudicatory,” meaning the water companies are entitled to a meaningful hearing before being deprived of their right to divert water from the two creeks.

    “Whether an action is legislative or adjudicatory turns on the character of the action, rather than its label,” U.S. Circuit Judge Lawrence VanDyke wrote. “Actions affecting large areas with undifferentiated populations are considered legislative.”.

    “By contrast, adjudicatory actions target or exceptionally affect a few persons on an individual basis,” the Donald Trump appointee added.

    While legislative regulations and orders don’t require individualized hearings, due process requires that adjudicative decisions provide notice and predeprivation hearings.

    “The reason for requiring hearings for adjudicatory but not legislative decisionmaking is fundamentally a practical one: As the Supreme Court explained, hearings become impracticable when the affected group is too large to give a direct voice in the adoption of a challenged regulation,” VanDyke said.

    In this case, 22 water rights holders along the Deer Creek and Mill Creek were affected by the 2021 emergency order to cut back their diversions, but the plaintiffs claim they were given only a five-minute public comment period, with no opportunity to cross-examine the state’s witnesses supporting the regulations.

    This, VanDyke stated, was not a meaningful hearing.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Circuit Judge John Owens, a Barack Obama appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Danielle Forrest, a Trump appointee, joined in the decision.

    In a separate memorandum disposition, the panel upheld the trial judge’s dismissal of the plaintiffs’ takings claims under the Fifth Amendment because they could have sought compensation for their losses through an inverse condemnation lawsuit in California state court.

    In a recent development, the appeal focused on water rights held in Mill Creek and Deer Creek in Tehama County. Those rights allow the companies to divert water for some 11,000 acres of land with orchards, pasture and other uses.

    In April 2021, after a lack of winter storms left the state’s water reservoirs depleted, California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a drought state of emergency, leading state agencies to take action and protect salmon, steelhead and other fish.

    Jackson Minasian, an attorney for the plaintiffs, argued at a hearing before the Ninth Circuit panel in August that California had stopped the diversions four times in seven years. The state will have future droughts and curtailment orders for the water, and when that happens, the attorney said, the companies should get a due process hearing and compensation for the taking of the water.

    Sources indicate that âThe salmon and steelhead come back every year,â Minasian noted. âTheyâre taking it for free and they keep doing it.â.

    Minasian and representatives of the California Attorney General’s Office didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

    Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson and the arc of the law

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion.
    • Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view.
    • Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Sources indicate that in September, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson received an award named after the late Justice William Brennan, a liberal lion. In her acceptance speech, Jackson discussed Brennan’s role as the Supreme Court became more conservative, noting that he “believed that even his dissents could make a difference and remind the nation that the pursuit of equal justice under law is an ongoing effort.” Jackson indicated that she agreed with that idea, telling the audience that she saw “dissent[s] as more than just a disagreement with the outcome of a case, I see them as an expression of faith in the future and a demonstration of hope.” As she put it, “However desolate the moment feels, we who write for a future age have hope that the noble and collective work of bending the long arc of the law toward justice will continue.”.

    Since joining the court in the summer of 2022, Jackson has sought to promote her understanding of that view. Although she has been consistently part of the court’s liberal bloc, even among the three Democratic appointees she has forged a unique role. As her invocation of Brennan suggests, it often appears that her goal is not simply to express disagreement with the majority, but to offer an alternative vision and to speak to the public directly – even if she does so without the support of her fellow liberals.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A federal judge rejected two nursesâ efforts to dismiss claims that their handling of Ben Cunninghamâs medical care at San Diego Central Jail contributed to his death weeks after he fell from a top bunk in a cell.

    SAN DIEGO (CN) âÂ A fall from a top bunk in a San Diego jail left a man suffering from alcoholism with potential injuries that may have caused his death a few weeks later.

    The nurses responsible for his care are still on the hook for a lawsuit filed by his family against San Diego County, a federal judge ruled.

    In a recent development, the family members of Ben Cunningham say the man was in the hospital for serious liver and kidney issues, but left â against medical advice â hours before police officers arrested him and took him to the San Diego Central Jail on Jan. 28, 2024. They say Cunningham should have been transported back to the hospital or placed in a medical observation bed at the jail.

    The family members say Cunningham was instead given a top bunk in a three-bunk bed in a jail cell, despite his disclosure of his serious medical needs and obvious inebriation. Cunningham fell from the top bunk a few hours later, lost consciousness and was unable to stand on his own, they say. But he was not taken to an emergency room until more than 24 hours later.

    According to recent reports, family members say the nurse who was in charge of his intake, Chasity Beene, and the nurse responsible for monitoring his condition after he fell, Brenda Bebal, contributed to his death. The family claims deliberate indifference to medical needs, negligence and wrongful death, among others.

    Industry observers note that beene argues the familyâs complaint does not establish her personal involvement in Cunninghamâs intake and falls short of federal pleading standards. She also notes the plaintiffsâ claims donât describe an intentional decision on her part.

    It has been revealed that U.S. District Judge Cathy Bencivengo disagreed.

    âThe allegations that Beene knew that decedent was detoxing and had existing medical problems, knew San Diego Central Jailâs relevant policies and procedures, and that a reasonable nurse practitioner would have known of the dangers in a similar situation, yet did not send decedent to the hospital, place him in a medical observation bed or flag him for a low bunk are sufficient to plausibly allege an intentional decision by Beene regarding decedentâs medical care,â Bencivengo, a Barack Obama appointee, wrote on Monday.

    âGiven the alleged policy and procedure, it is plausible that a reasonable nurse practitioner performing decedentâs medical evaluation âwould have appreciated the high degree of risk involvedâ and, at a minimum, flagged him for a low bunk,â she continued. âBeeneâs decision not to order any of these three treatment options does not transform her actions into something unintentional.â.

    Industry observers note that cunninghamâs family says Bebal ordered only that his vitals be checked every other day after his fall. As a result, there was an unreasonably long delay in taking him to the hospital, which caused his death, they say.

    Bebal argues the symptoms of serious harm did not develop until after her evaluation, so she was unaware of them.

    âThis argument mischaracterizes plaintiffsâ allegations,â the judge wrote. âPlaintiffs do not allege that these later symptoms are what signaled the substantial risk of serious harm, but that the immediate effects of the fall â decedent hitting his head, his loss of consciousness and his inability to stand â put Bebal on notice of a substantial risk of serious harm. Plaintiffs also claim that Bebal did not conduct a real evaluation of decedent and that given the fall and decedentâs medical history, Bebalâs decision not to conduct a more thorough evaluation is what also put decedent at a substantial risk of serious harm.â.

    The nurses both argue the claims against them were untimely because they were filed more than a year after Cunningham died, but Bencivengo disagreed with this too. They filed their lawsuit within a year of his death certificate being issued, she ruled.

    The plaintiffs originally believed Cunningham had been beaten by cellmates or corrections officers.

    Attorneys for the family members said they were pleased with the ruling.

    “We, including Ben’s loved ones, are heartened and validated by the court’s ruling,” attorney Kauren In proceeding forward on all claims, we hope that Ben’s case will be a lesson to the County and for-profit contractors such as Naphcare and Correctional Healthcare Partners that medical providers and deputies must begin to work as a team and treat the safety of people in the County jails as their top priority.

    The family members also named the San Diego County Sheriffâs Office, its deputies and medical officers in their lawsuit.

    Spokespersons for the defendants did not respond to requests for comment.
